title: 09 — Azure Storage
html:
09 — Azure Storage

One storage account gives you four services. Blob is the one you'll use most; the others matter less than people assume.

1. The four services in one account

Service Model Use for Don't use for
Blob Object store: container → blob ⭐ Files, images, documents, backups, data lake, static sites, logs Anything needing queries
Queue Simple FIFO-ish message queue Cheap background work Ordering, transactions, DLQ (use Service Bus — file 08)
Table Key-value / wide-column NoSQL Cheap high-volume simple lookups by PartitionKey+RowKey Anything relational or query-heavy — use Cosmos DB for new work 🔄
File SMB/NFS network share Lift-and-shift apps needing a file share New cloud-native apps (use Blob)

Account types 🔄: StorageV2 (general purpose v2) for almost everything; Premium block blob for high-transaction, low-latency workloads; ADLS Gen2 (StorageV2 + hierarchical namespace) for analytics — it gives you real directories and POSIX-style ACLs, and it's what Databricks/Synapse/Fabric expect.

⚠️ Hierarchical namespace can only be enabled at account creation. Choosing wrong means creating a new account and copying everything.

2. Redundancy — pick deliberately, it's hard to change

Option Copies Survives Cost
LRS 3 in one datacentre A disk/rack failure £
ZRS 3 across availability zones ⭐ A datacentre failure ££
GRS LRS + 3 async in the paired region A regional failure (with failover) £££
GZRS ZRS + async to the paired region Both ££££
RA-GRS / RA-GZRS + read access to the secondary Read during a regional outage +£

💡 ZRS for production as the baseline. Add GRS/GZRS only where the data genuinely can't be regenerated and the business accepts the cost. ⚠️ GRS replication is asynchronous — a regional failover can lose the last few minutes of writes, and failover is customer-initiated with a real RPO. It is not a magic "no data loss" button.

3. Blob storage

3.1 Structure and types

Storage account (globally unique DNS name)
└── Container ("folder" — but flat; there are no real directories without HNS)
    └── Blob   "reports/2026/07/portfolio-42.pdf"  ← the slashes are just part of the NAME
Blob type Use
Block blob ⭐ Everything normal: files, images, documents, backups
Append blob Log files — append-only writes
Page blob Random-access 512-byte pages — VM disks. You'll rarely create one

3.2 Access tiers

Tier Storage cost Access cost Minimum retention 🔄 Retrieval
Hot Highest Lowest — Instant
Cool Lower Higher 30 days Instant
Cold Lower still Higher still 90 days Instant
Archive Lowest Highest 180 days ⚠️ Hours to rehydrate

⚠️ Two traps: early deletion from Cool/Cold/Archive incurs a prorated early-deletion charge for the remaining minimum period; and Archive blobs cannot be read at all until rehydrated (standard priority: up to ~15 hours). Never archive anything a user might request interactively.

// Lifecycle management — set this on day one, not after the bill arrives
resource lifecycle 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/managementPolicies@2023-01-01' = {
  parent: storage
  name: 'default'
  properties: {
    policy: {
      rules: [{
        name: 'tier-and-expire-reports'
        enabled: true
        type: 'Lifecycle'
        definition: {
          filters: { blobTypes: ['blockBlob'], prefixMatch: ['reports/'] }
          actions: {
            baseBlob: {
              tierToCool:    { daysAfterModificationGreaterThan: 30 }
              tierToArchive: { daysAfterModificationGreaterThan: 180 }
              delete:        { daysAfterModificationGreaterThan: 2555 }   // 7 years
            }
            snapshot: { delete: { daysAfterCreationGreaterThan: 90 } }
            version:  { delete: { daysAfterCreationGreaterThan: 90 } }
          }
        }
      }]
    }
  }
}

💡 Lifecycle policies are the highest-ROI storage cost lever. Most accounts hold years of blobs nobody has read since the week they were written.

3.3 Data protection features — enable these

Feature Protects against
Soft delete (blobs + containers) ⭐ Accidental deletion. Retention 7–365 days
Versioning Overwrites — every write creates a version
Point-in-time restore Bulk restore of a container to a timestamp (requires versioning + change feed)
Immutable storage / legal hold Regulatory WORM requirements
Change feed An ordered log of all changes — useful for downstream processing

⚠️ Versioning + no lifecycle policy on versions = unbounded cost growth. Every overwrite keeps the old bytes forever. Always pair versioning with a version-expiry rule (see the policy above).

4. ⭐ Authentication: use Entra ID, not keys

Method Verdict
Entra ID + managed identity (RBAC) ⭐ Use this. No secret, per-identity audit, revocable, granular
User delegation SAS ⭐ Best SAS type — signed with an Entra credential, so it's revocable and attributable
Service SAS / Account SAS Signed with the account key — inherits all its problems
Account keys ⚠️ Two keys, full control of everything, frequently pasted into config and chat. Disable them 
resource storage 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-05-01' = {
  name: 'stshopprod'
  sku: { name: 'Standard_ZRS' }
  kind: 'StorageV2'
  properties: {
    allowSharedKeyAccess: false          // ⭐ disable account keys entirely
    allowBlobPublicAccess: false         // ⭐ no anonymous containers
    minimumTlsVersion: 'TLS1_2'
    supportsHttpsTrafficOnly: true
    publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'      // with a private endpoint
    networkAcls: { defaultAction: 'Deny', bypass: 'AzureServices' }
  }
}

Then grant the data-plane role — remembering that Contributor on the account is not enough (file 04 §3):

Role Grants
Storage Blob Data Reader Read blobs
Storage Blob Data Contributor Read/write/delete blobs
Storage Blob Data Owner + POSIX ACLs (ADLS Gen2)
Storage Queue Data Contributor Queue messages
Storage Table Data Contributor Table entities 
// Registration — singleton client, managed identity
builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.AddBlobServiceClient(new Uri($"https://{accountName}.blob.core.windows.net"));
    clients.UseCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential());
});

5. SAS tokens — when you genuinely need them

A SAS is a signed URL granting scoped, time-limited access — how you let a browser upload or download directly, without proxying bytes through your API.

public async Task<Uri> CreateDownloadUrlAsync(string container, string blobName, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var blobClient = _blobServiceClient.GetBlobContainerClient(container).GetBlobClient(blobName);

    // ⭐ USER DELEGATION SAS — signed with an Entra key, not the account key.
    // Revocable, attributable in logs, and works with allowSharedKeyAccess = false.
    var startsOn = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMinutes(-5);      // clock-skew tolerance
    var expiresOn = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMinutes(15);     // ⭐ SHORT

    var userDelegationKey = await _blobServiceClient
        .GetUserDelegationKeyAsync(startsOn, expiresOn, ct);

    var builder = new BlobSasBuilder
    {
        BlobContainerName = container,
        BlobName = blobName,
        Resource = "b",
        StartsOn = startsOn,
        ExpiresOn = expiresOn,
        Protocol = SasProtocol.Https,
        ContentDisposition = $"attachment; filename=\"{Sanitise(blobName)}\"",
    };
    builder.SetPermissions(BlobSasPermissions.Read);          // read only

    var sas = builder.ToSasQueryParameters(userDelegationKey.Value, _accountName);
    return new UriBuilder(blobClient.Uri) { Query = sas.ToString() }.Uri;
}

⚠️ SAS rules that are broken constantly:

  1. Short expiry. Minutes, not days. A leaked SAS is valid until it expires and cannot otherwise be revoked (unless it's a user-delegation SAS, where revoking the delegation key kills it).
  2. Minimum permissions. Read-only for downloads; write-only (Create/Write, no Read, no Delete) for uploads.
  3. HTTPS only.
  4. Never generate a SAS from an account key — use user delegation.
  5. ⚠️ A SAS URL in a log, a referrer header, or a browser history is a leaked credential. Prefer POST-returned URLs over URLs embedded in pages that get shared.
  6. Stored access policies on a container give you a revocation handle for service SAS tokens.

💡 The direct-upload pattern (this decision determines whether your service scales):

Client → POST /api/documents/upload-url   → API returns a short-lived write SAS
Client → PUT directly to blob storage      ← bytes NEVER pass through your API
Client → POST /api/documents/confirm       → API verifies the blob exists and records metadata

Proxying a 500 MB upload through an App Service instance consumes memory, a thread, and request timeout budget for no benefit.

6. Using the SDK properly

public sealed class DocumentStore(BlobServiceClient blobServiceClient, ILogger<DocumentStore> logger)
{
    private const string ContainerName = "documents";

    public async Task<Uri> UploadAsync(
        string blobName, Stream content, string contentType, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var container = blobServiceClient.GetBlobContainerClient(ContainerName);
        var blob = container.GetBlobClient(blobName);

        await blob.UploadAsync(content, new BlobUploadOptions
        {
            HttpHeaders = new BlobHttpHeaders
            {
                ContentType = contentType,
                CacheControl = "private, max-age=3600",
            },
            Metadata = new Dictionary<string, string>
            {
                ["uploadedBy"] = "shop-api",
                ["uploadedAt"] = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToString("O"),
            },
            // Optimistic concurrency: fail if the blob already exists
            Conditions = new BlobRequestConditions { IfNoneMatch = ETag.All },
            TransferOptions = new StorageTransferOptions
            {
                MaximumConcurrency = 4,                    // parallel block upload
                InitialTransferSize = 8 * 1024 * 1024,
            },
        }, ct);

        return blob.Uri;
    }

    // ⭐ Stream — never ReadAllBytes a large blob into memory
    public async Task<Stream> OpenReadAsync(string blobName, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var blob = blobServiceClient.GetBlobContainerClient(ContainerName).GetBlobClient(blobName);
        return await blob.OpenReadAsync(cancellationToken: ct);
    }

    // Efficient listing with paging and a prefix
    public async IAsyncEnumerable<BlobItem> ListAsync(
        string prefix, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        var container = blobServiceClient.GetBlobContainerClient(ContainerName);
        await foreach (var page in container
            .GetBlobsAsync(BlobTraits.None, BlobStates.None, prefix, ct)
            .AsPages(pageSizeHint: 500).WithCancellation(ct))
        {
            foreach (var item in page.Values) yield return item;
        }
    }
}

Rules:

  1. ⭐ BlobServiceClient is thread-safe and expensive — register it as a singleton. A new client per request is the same class of bug as new HttpClient().
  2. Stream, don't buffer. OpenReadAsync/OpenWriteAsync for anything that might be large.
  3. The SDK retries transient failures already — don't wrap it in your own retry loop.
  4. Use ETag conditions for optimistic concurrency (IfMatch on update, IfNoneMatch = ETag.All on create-if-absent).
  5. Set ContentType or browsers will download your PDFs as octet-streams.
  6. Blob names are case-sensitive, and slashes are just characters (unless HNS is on).

7. Performance and scale targets

🔄 Approximate, verify current limits:

Limit Value
Max storage account capacity 5 PiB
Max request rate per account ~20,000 requests/s
Max ingress/egress per account 10s of Gbps, region-dependent
Max block blob size ~190 TiB
Single blob throughput Up to ~60 MiB/s (Standard)

Scaling techniques:

  • Partition across accounts if you exceed the per-account limits — hash the tenant or entity id.
  • ⚠️ Avoid sequential naming prefixes (20260727-0001, 20260727-0002…). Blob storage partitions by name range, so sequential prefixes concentrate load on one partition server. Prefix with a hash or use a naturally distributed key.
  • Parallelise large transfers (StorageTransferOptions) and use azcopy for bulk moves.
  • Put a CDN or Front Door in front of frequently read public blobs — cheaper and faster than egressing from storage every time.
  • Premium block blob for high-transaction, low-latency workloads (it's priced by transaction rather than by GB, so it wins for small hot objects).

8. Networking and security

✅ allowSharedKeyAccess: false        — Entra only
✅ allowBlobPublicAccess: false       — no anonymous containers
✅ minimumTlsVersion: TLS1_2
✅ supportsHttpsTrafficOnly: true
✅ publicNetworkAccess: Disabled + private endpoint (+ the privatelink DNS zone!)
✅ networkAcls.defaultAction: Deny
✅ Soft delete + versioning enabled
✅ Diagnostic settings → Log Analytics
✅ Defender for Storage enabled (malware scanning, anomaly detection)

⚠️ allowBlobPublicAccess: true plus a container set to public is how storage accounts end up indexed by search engines. Disable it at the account level so no one can enable it per container.

Private endpoints: each storage service needs its own private endpoint (blob, queue, table, file are separate sub-resources) and its own private DNS zone (privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, etc.). ⚠️ Missing the DNS zone is the classic failure — the name resolves publicly and the connection times out.

Customer-managed keys (CMK): encryption at rest is on by default with Microsoft-managed keys; CMK in Key Vault is for regulatory requirements. ⚠️ If the key is deleted or access is revoked, the account becomes inaccessible — enable purge protection on the vault.

9. Table Storage vs Cosmos DB

Table Storage Cosmos DB (Table API)
Cost ⭐ Very cheap Higher (provisioned RUs)
Latency ~10s of ms Single-digit ms, SLA-backed
Indexing PartitionKey + RowKey only Automatic on all properties
Global distribution ✘ ✔
Throughput Best-effort Guaranteed

💡 Use Table Storage when the access pattern is genuinely a point lookup by PartitionKey+RowKey, cost matters, and you can tolerate variable latency. Use Cosmos DB for anything else — the moment you need to query by a non-key property, Table Storage forces a full scan.

Design rules if you do use it: PartitionKey chosen for even distribution and to match your queries; RowKey for ordering within the partition (⚠️ it sorts as a string — zero-pad numbers and use reverse-ticks for descending time); a point query (PartitionKey + RowKey) is the only fast operation; entities are limited to 1 MB and 255 properties.

10. Azure Files (briefly)

An SMB/NFS share. Use it for lift-and-shift applications that require a file share, shared configuration across VMs, or container persistent volumes.

Tier Notes
Standard (transaction-optimised / hot / cool) HDD-backed, pay per GB + transactions
Premium SSD-backed, provisioned IOPS, low latency

Azure File Sync caches a share on Windows Servers with cloud tiering — the standard hybrid file-server modernisation path.

💡 For a new cloud-native .NET app, use Blob rather than Files. Files exists to avoid rewriting applications that assume a drive letter.

11. Monitoring, cost, and troubleshooting

Metrics to watch: transactions (by API and response type), ingress/egress, availability, success E2E latency vs success server latency (the gap is network/client time), and used capacity by tier.

Cost drivers, in order: storage volume by tier, transactions (often larger than the storage cost for chatty workloads), egress, early-deletion charges, and version/snapshot accumulation.

Symptom Cause
403 AuthorizationPermissionMismatch Missing the data-plane RBAC role (Contributor isn't enough), or RBAC hasn't propagated
403 AuthenticationFailed with a SAS Expired, clock skew, wrong permissions, or allowSharedKeyAccess: false with a key-signed SAS
409 BlobAlreadyExists An IfNoneMatch condition — usually intentional
412 ConditionNotMet ETag mismatch — someone else wrote first (optimistic concurrency working correctly)
503 ServerBusy / throttling Exceeding partition or account limits — check for a sequential naming hot spot
Times out from App Service, works from a VM Private endpoint without the private DNS zone
Costs climbing with no new data Versioning or snapshots with no lifecycle expiry

🧪

az storage blob list --account-name stshopprod -c documents --auth-mode login -o table
az storage account show -n stshopprod --query "{sku:sku.name, https:supportsHttpsTrafficOnly, sharedKey:allowSharedKeyAccess}"

12. Checklist

  • ZRS (or GZRS) redundancy in production
  • allowSharedKeyAccess: false — Entra ID + managed identity only
  • allowBlobPublicAccess: false, TLS 1.2 minimum, HTTPS only
  • Data-plane RBAC roles granted (not just Contributor)
  • Private endpoint + private DNS zone if public access is disabled
  • Soft delete (blobs and containers) + versioning enabled
  • Lifecycle policy tiering and expiring blobs, snapshots, and versions
  • BlobServiceClient registered as a singleton
  • Large files streamed, never buffered into memory
  • Direct client upload/download via short-lived user-delegation SAS, not proxied through the API
  • SAS: minutes-long expiry, minimum permissions, HTTPS only, never key-signed
  • Blob names avoid sequential prefixes that create partition hot spots
  • ContentType and Content-Disposition set on user-facing blobs
  • Diagnostic settings to Log Analytics; Defender for Storage enabled
  • Cost reviewed: transactions and egress, not just capacity

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • How do you let a browser upload a 1 GB file? A short-lived write-only user-delegation SAS so the client uploads directly to Blob Storage; the API only issues the URL and records metadata afterwards. Proxying the bytes through the API wastes memory and threads and doesn't scale.
  • Account key vs SAS vs Entra ID? Full control and unrevocable / scoped and time-limited but still key-derived unless it's a user-delegation SAS / per-identity, auditable, revocable — use Entra.
  • Why did my app get 403 after I gave it Contributor on the storage account? Contributor is control plane; blob access needs Storage Blob Data Contributor on the data plane.
  • Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive? Decreasing storage cost, increasing access cost and minimum retention; Archive needs hours to rehydrate, so never use it for interactive data.
  • How do you control storage costs? Lifecycle policies, expiring versions and snapshots, watching transactions and egress (often bigger than capacity), and a CDN in front of hot public content.
  • What causes storage throttling? Exceeding account/partition limits — commonly a sequential blob-naming scheme concentrating load on one partition range.
